The complainant thereafter approached Police Station Maharajpura and narrated the incident, but the Station House Officer allegedly informed her that since an FIR in relation to the dowry dispute had already been registered, no further FIR would be lodged.

The learned Revisional Court, vide impugned order dated 07.07.2025,

sentences.text: It is submitted that while exercising revisional jurisdiction under Section 397 read with Section 401 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, the Revisional Court was bound to comply with the mandate of sub-section (2) of Section 401 of the Code, which expressly provides that no order to the prejudice of the accused or any other person shall be made unless he has had an opportunity of being heard either personally or by pleader in his own defence.

The petitioners, being the persons directly prejudiced by the impugned revisional order inasmuch as the said order culminated in a direction for registration of FIR against them were entitled to an effective opportunity of hearing before the Revisional Court.

However, admittedly, no such opportunity was afforded to the present petitioners before setting aside NEUTRAL CITATION NO. 2026:MPHC-GWL:7588 5 MCRC-36345-2025 the well-reasoned order of the learned JMFC dated 08.05.2025 and directing action under Section 156(3) of the Code.
The failure to grant an opportunity of hearing strikes at the very root of the revisional proceedings and renders the impugned order legally unsustainable.

5. It is further submitted that the Hon'ble Supreme Court in Santhakumari and Ors. v. State of Tamil Nadu and Anr. reported in (2023) 15 SCC 440 has categorically held that in a criminal revision arising out of proceedings under Section 156(3) of the Code, where the order is likely to prejudice the proposed accused, an opportunity of hearing is mandatory in view of Section 401(2) Cr.P.C. An order which would adversely affect the rights of a person suspected of having committed the offence,
compliance with the principles of natural justice and statutory mandate is indispensable.

Similarly,
the Hon'ble High Court of Allahabad in Jagannath Verma And Ors. vs The State Of U.P. reported in AIR 2014 ALLAHABAD 214, has authoritatively laid down that an order passed by a Magistrate rejecting an application under Section 156(3) of the Code for registration of a case and investigation is not an interlocutory order and is amenable to revisional jurisdiction under Section 397 Cr.P.C.

The ratio of the said judgment squarely applies to the facts of the present case.

The order rejecting an application under Section 156(3) is not an interlocutory order but a final order insofar as the rights of the complainant at that stage are concerned, and therefore, it is revisable under Section 397 Cr.P.C.

However, once the revisional jurisdiction was invoked by the complainant, and the Revisional Court proposed to reverse the order and direct action which would result in registration of an FIR against the present petitioners, the petitioners acquired a valuable right of hearing under Section 401(2) Cr.P.C.

The impugned order,
therefore, stands vitiated on account of violation of principles of natural justice as well as non-compliance with the mandatory provisions of Section 401(2) Cr.P.C.

In view of the aforesaid submissions, it is prayed that this Hon'ble Court, in exercise of its inherent jurisdiction, may be pleased to set aside the impugned order dated 07.07.2025 passed by the learned 22nd Additional Sessions Judge, Gwalior in Criminal Revision No.175/2025 and the consequential order dated NEUTRAL CITATION NO. 2026:MPHC-GWL:7588 7 MCRC-36345-2025 17.07.2025 passed by the learned JMFC, Gwalior.

8. Per contra, learned counsel for the State submits that the present petition is devoid of merits and is liable to be dismissed at the threshold, inasmuch as the impugned order dated 07.07.2025 passed by the learned Revisional Court and the consequential order dated 17.07.2025 passed by the learned JMFC merely direct registration of an FIR in exercise of powers under Section 156(3) of the Code,
which is a pre-cognizance stage, and the stage of taking cognizance has not yet commenced.

It is contended that at the stage of directing investigation under Section 156(3) Cr.P.C., the proposed accused has no vested right of hearing, as the proceedings are only meant to set the criminal law in motion and to ensure a fair and proper investigation.

The revisional court, while examining the correctness of the order rejecting the application under Section 156(3), was concerned only with the legality and propriety of the Magistrate's refusal to order investigation, and the direction issued does not determine the guilt or otherwise of the petitioners.

It is further submitted that registration of FIR does not ipso facto prejudice the petitioners, who will have adequate opportunity to put forth their defence at the appropriate stage in accordance with law, and therefore, the plea of violation of Section 401(2) Cr.P.C. is misconceived.
The State accordingly submits that no case for interference in exercise of inherent jurisdiction is made out.
9. Learned Counsel for respondent No. 1 submits that the present proceedings are wholly misconceived and are not maintainable in law.

It is a settled proposition that a proposed accused,
against whom an application NEUTRAL CITATION NO. 2026:MPHC-GWL:7588 8 MCRC-36345-2025 under Section 156(3) of the Code of Criminal Procedure is moved, has no right of hearing either at the stage of consideration of the said application by the learned Magistrate or at the stage of any proceedings arising therefrom, including revision before the revisional court.

The scheme of the Code makes it abundantly clear that prior to the stage of summoning, a person against whom allegations are made does not acquire the status of an accused entitled to participate in the proceedings.

10. It is further submitted that the Hon'ble Apex Court has affirmed the judgment rendered by this Hon'ble Court in the case of Father Thomas Vs. State of U.P. reported in 2011 (72) ACC 564 (Allahabad) (Full Bench) , wherein it has been categorically held that an accused has no right to be heard before he is summoned by the Court under the Code of Criminal Procedure.

sentences.text: The Full Bench authoritatively declared that till the stage of summoning, the person against whom allegations are levelled has no right to raise any objection and consequently cannot claim a right to challenge any order passed under Section 156(3) Cr.P.C. prior to his summoning.
The law laid down therein has attained finality and is binding.

It is also well established that an order passed by the Magistrate under Section 156(3) Cr.P.C., directing the police to register a First Information Report and to investigate the matter, is an interlocutory order in nature.

4 rights of the parties nor it adjudicates upon the guilt or innocence of any individual.

Therefore, in view of the bar contained under Section 397(2) Cr.P.C., a revision against such an order is NEUTRAL CITATION NO. 2026:MPHC-GWL:7588 9 MCRC-36345-2025 not maintainable.
In the present case, the learned Magistrate exercised jurisdiction vested under Section 156(3) Cr.P.C. and directed registration of the FIR and investigation.
At this preliminary stage, the petitioners being only a proposed accused, had no vested or statutory right to be heard.
In light of the aforesaid settled principles of law, it is submitted that the revision petition deserves to be dismissed at the threshold.

11. Heard counsel for the parties and perused the record.
12.

The controversy involved in the present petition lies in a narrow compass, as to whether the learned Revisional Court could have set aside the order of the learned JMFC rejecting the application under Section 156(3) Cr.P.C. and directing action thereunder without affording an opportunity of hearing to the present petitioners, who stand directly prejudiced by such order.

13. It is not in dispute that the learned JMFC, Gwalior had, upon due consideration of the allegations and the material placed on record, rejected the application under Section 156(3) Cr.P.C.
vide order dated 08.05.2025.
The said order was assailed by respondent No.1 before the learned 22nd Additional Sessions Judge, Gwalior in Criminal Revision No.175/2025.

By the impugned order dated 07.07.2025, the learned Revisional Court allowed the revision, set aside the order of the learned JMFC and remanded the matter with a direction to proceed in accordance with Section 156(3) Cr.P.C., which ultimately culminated in the order dated 17.07.2025 directing registration of FIR and the consequent registration of Crime No.451/2025 against the present petitioners.
NEUTRAL CITATION NO. 2026:MPHC-GWL:7588 10 MCRC-36345-2025 14.

The pivotal question thus is whether such an order, which results in registration of an FIR against identified individuals, could have been passed in revision without affording them an opportunity of hearing.
Sub-section (2) of Section 401 Cr.P.C.

in clear and unambiguous terms mandates that no order to the prejudice of the accused or any other person shall be made by the Revisional Court unless he has had an opportunity of being heard either personally or by pleader in his own defence.
The expression "any other person" employed in the provision is of wide amplitude and is not confined only to a person who has already been summoned as an accused.
The legislative intent is to ensure adherence to the principles of natural justice wherever a revisional order is likely to adversely affect the rights of a person.

15. The Hon'ble Supreme Court in Santhakumari (supra) has categorically held that in a criminal revision arising out of proceedings under Section 156(3) Cr.P.C., where the order is likely to prejudice the proposed accused, compliance with Section 401(2) Cr.P.C. is mandatory and an opportunity of hearing must be afforded.

It has been observed that even at a pre-cognizance stage, if the revisional order has the effect of adversely impacting the rights of a person suspected of having committed the offence, the statutory mandate cannot be diluted.

The Hon'ble High Court of Allahabad in Jagannath Verma (supra) has authoritatively held that an order passed by a Magistrate Sunil Singh Bhadouriya vs Smt Priyanka Singh Bhadauriya on 26 February, 2026 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/87873769/
5 rejecting an application under Section 156(3) Cr.P.C. for registration of a case and investigation is not an interlocutory order and is, therefore, amenable to revisional jurisdiction under Section 397 Cr.P.C.

entities.text: Sunil Singh Bhadouriya vs Smt Priyanka Singh Bhadauriya
entities.label: PRECEDENT

sentences.text:
The Court further held that when such a revision is entertained and the NEUTRAL CITATION NO. 2026:MPHC-GWL:7588 11 MCRC-36345-2025 revisional court proposes to pass an order which may result in registration of an FIR or otherwise adversely affect the person named in the complaint, the bar contained under Section 401(2) Cr.P.C. squarely applies and an opportunity of hearing to the prospective accused is mandatory.
16.
In the present case, the impugned revisional order has directly resulted in a direction for registration of FIR against the petitioners.
Such a direction cannot be said to be innocuous.
Registration of an FIR entails investigation, possible arrest, and other coercive steps permissible under law.
Therefore, it cannot be gainsaid that the order passed by the Revisional Court is to the clear prejudice of the present petitioners.
In such circumstances, the requirement of affording them an opportunity of hearing under Section 401(2) Cr.P.C. was mandatory.

17. The contention advanced on behalf of the State and respondent No.1 that at the stage of Section 156(3) Cr.P.C. the proposed accused has no right of hearing before the Magistrate, though supported by judicial precedents, does not answer the issue arising in the present case.

The question here is not of hearing before the Magistrate at the stage of consideration of the application under Section 156(3)
Cr.P.C., but of compliance with the statutory mandate governing revisional jurisdiction.

Once the matter entered the revisional domain and the Revisional Court proposed to reverse an order in a manner prejudicial to identified persons, the embargo contained in Section 401(2) Cr.P.C. came into full operation.

18. Admittedly, in the case at hand, no notice was issued to the present petitioners and no opportunity of hearing was afforded to them before NEUTRAL CITATION NO.
2026:MPHC-GWL:7588 12 MCRC-36345-2025 passing the impugned order dated 07.07.2025.
The order, therefore, stands vitiated on account of non-compliance with the mandatory requirement of Section 401(2) Cr.P.C. as well as violation of principles of natural justice.
The consequential order dated 17.07.2025 passed by the learned JMFC directing registration of FIR, being a direct outcome of the said revisional order, cannot survive independently.
19. Accordingly, the petition succeeds and is allowed.

The impugned order dated 07.07.2025 passed by the learned 22nd Additional Sessions Judge, Gwalior in Criminal Revision No.175/2025 and the consequential order dated 17.07.2025 passed by the learned JMFC, Gwalior are hereby set aside.

The matter is remanded back to the learned Revisional Court to decide Criminal Revision No.175/2025 afresh in accordance with law after impleading the present petitioners as parties and affording them a reasonable opportunity of hearing.
20. It is clarified that this Court has not expressed any opinion on the merits of the allegations and all issues are left open to be decided by the Revisional Court independently.
